summary: Ghana's capital is the spiritual home of the African diaspora. With English as the official language, a Right of Abode pathway for people of African descent, and the energy of the Year of Return movement, Accra draws more Black diaspora returnees than any city on this list.
dataSource: Numbeo, Nomad List, US State Dept, field research

internet.reliabilityNotes: Power outages (dumsor) affect connectivity in some neighborhoods. Coworking spaces typically have generators and stable fiber.

safety.keyNotes: Accra is generally safe for tourists and diaspora returnees. Petty theft and vehicle crime exist in crowded areas. Violent crime against foreigners is rare.

weather.rainySeasonMonths: April to June and September to October
weather.climateNotes: Hot and humid year-round. Harmattan winds from the Sahara bring drier, hazy conditions from December to February.

visaEase.usPassport: Visa required. e-Visa available online. $60 for 60 days.
visaEase.specialNote: People of African descent can apply for the Right of Abode, granting indefinite stay rights in Ghana. Processing takes 3-6 months. This is Ghana's most powerful draw for diaspora returnees.

expatCommunity.estimatedSize: 5,000 to 8,000 expats plus a large African-American diaspora returnee community

keyFacts: Ghana is the only country in Africa offering a formal Right of Abode pathway for people of African descent, granting indefinite residency
The Year of Return (2019) and Beyond the Return program brought over 500,000 diaspora visitors and sparked a permanent returnee community
English is the official language, eliminating the language barrier that affects most other African cities on this list
Accra has the most direct flights from Atlanta, New York, and London of any sub-Saharan city, with direct Delta service to Atlanta daily
whyItMatters: No city on this list carries more emotional weight for the African-American diaspora than Accra. The Year of Return was not a marketing campaign; it was a reckoning. Tens of thousands came and thousands stayed. For Black Americans, Caribbeans, and Afro-Europeans looking for a place that actively wants them and has built infrastructure to receive them, Accra is unmatched. The Right of Abode program, the English language environment, the deep Ghanaian-American ties, and the growing returnee business community make Accra the most culturally resonant base on the continent. Its infrastructure challenges (power, internet, traffic) are real but manageable, and they are improving.
